sections.title: Foods to Prioritise
sections.description: These foods support hormonal balance, reduce inflammation, and help stabilise blood sugar — all key for managing PMOS.

cards.title: Eat More Leafy Greens
cards.body: Water leaf, bitter leaf, njama-njama, and moringa are packed with iron, folate, and antioxidants. Add at least one portion to every meal. These greens reduce the inflammation that makes PMOS worse.

cards.title: Choose Low-GI Starches
cards.body: Unripe plantain, local red rice, and oat-based fufu release energy slowly. This prevents the blood sugar spikes that worsen insulin resistance — a key driver of PMOS symptoms.

cards.title: Beans and Legumes Daily
cards.body: Beans, lentils, and groundnuts are high in fibre and protein. They keep you full, lower cholesterol, and stabilise blood sugar. Koki (bean cake) is a great PMOS-friendly snack.

cards.title: Oily Fish Twice a Week
cards.body: Mackerel, tilapia, and smoked fish (canda) contain omega-3 fatty acids that reduce inflammation. Omega-3 also improves insulin sensitivity, which is directly beneficial for PMOS.

cards.title: Safou and Avocado for Healthy Fats
cards.body: Safou (African pear) and avocado provide monounsaturated fats that support hormone production. These healthy fats do not spike blood sugar and reduce systemic inflammation.

sections.title: Foods to Limit
sections.description: These foods can worsen insulin resistance and inflammation. You do not need to remove them entirely — smaller portions and less frequent eating makes a real difference.

cards.title: Reduce Cassava Fufu and White Rice
cards.body: Cassava fufu and white rice have a high glycaemic index (GI). They cause rapid blood sugar spikes followed by crashes — this worsens insulin resistance in PMOS. Switch to unripe plantain fufu or red rice.

cards.title: Cut Back on Fried Foods
cards.body: Puff puff, chin chin, and fried plantain add a lot of unhealthy fat. Deep frying increases inflammation. Try boiling, grilling, or steaming instead — the flavour of Cameroonian food still shines.

cards.title: Replace Sugary Drinks with Water or Herbal Teas
cards.body: Soft drinks and sweetened juices cause immediate insulin spikes and contribute to weight gain around the belly — a common PMOS symptom. Replace with water, zobo (hibiscus tea), or ginger tea.

cards.title: Swap Processed Snacks
cards.body: Biscuits and packaged snacks are made from refined flour and added sugar. They spike blood sugar quickly. Swap them for roasted groundnuts, garden egg salad, or a handful of beans.

sections.title: Simple Meal Ideas
sections.description: Quick Cameroonian meal combinations that are naturally balanced for PMOS management.

cards.title: PMOS-Friendly Breakfasts
cards.body:
• Boiled eggs with roasted plantain and zobo tea
• Oat porridge with guava and a handful of groundnuts
• Beans and plantain (beans ndolé with unripe plantain)
• Soya milk with a boiled sweet potato

Avoid: Bread with jam, sweetened cereals, sugary tea.

cards.title: PMOS-Friendly Lunches
cards.body:
• Unripe plantain fufu with egusi soup and smoked fish
• Red rice with eru soup and crayfish
• Ndolé with grilled chicken and boiled cocoyam
• Koki with grilled fish and garden egg salad

Key: always add plenty of leafy greens to your soup.

cards.title: PMOS-Friendly Dinners
cards.body:
• Light eru soup with one cup of oat fufu
• Grilled tilapia with steamed water leaf and boiled unripe plantain
• Beans pepper soup with a small portion of boiled yam
• Mbanga soup (small palm oil) with smoked fish and unripe plantain

Keep dinner lighter than lunch if possible.

cards.title: Smart Snacks Between Meals
cards.body:
• A handful of roasted groundnuts
• Garden egg with groundnut dip
• Roasted corn with a glass of water
• Koki (bean cake) — a filling, protein-rich snack
• A cup of guava or passion fruit

Snacking on protein and fibre prevents blood sugar dips that cause cravings.

sections.title: General Lifestyle Tips
sections.description: Small daily habits that work alongside your diet to manage PMOS symptoms effectively.

cards.title: Eat at Regular Times
cards.body: Try to eat breakfast, lunch, and dinner at roughly the same times each day. Skipping meals — especially breakfast — causes blood sugar drops that trigger insulin spikes when you eventually eat. Even a light breakfast helps regulate your hormones for the day.

cards.title: Use the Plate Method
cards.body:
At each meal, aim for:
• Half your plate: vegetables and leafy greens
• One quarter: lean protein (fish, beans, eggs)
• One quarter: low-GI starch (unripe plantain, red rice)

This simple guide naturally manages your blood sugar without counting anything.

cards.title: Drink 6–8 Glasses of Water Daily
cards.body: Water helps flush excess hormones from the body and supports kidney function. Start the day with a glass of warm water with ginger or lemon. Replace soft drinks with water, zobo, or herbal teas throughout the day.

cards.title: Walk for 30 Minutes Most Days
cards.body: Walking after meals is one of the most effective ways to lower blood sugar without medication. Even a 20-minute walk after lunch or dinner reduces post-meal glucose spikes. Aim for 150 minutes of moderate movement per week.

cards.title: Manage Stress and Sleep Well
cards.body: Chronic stress raises cortisol, which directly worsens insulin resistance and disrupts the menstrual cycle in PMOS. Aim for 7–8 hours of sleep. Simple practices like prayer, deep breathing, or a short walk outdoors in the evening can significantly reduce stress.

cards.title: Cook Smarter, Not Harder
cards.body:
The way food is cooked matters:
• Boil or steam starches instead of frying
• Use palm oil sparingly — 1–2 tablespoons per pot of soup is enough
• Add more vegetables to your soups to increase fibre and reduce the starch portion
• Cook beans from scratch rather than from tins when possible
